language.howToChooseYourGradeIntro: Our curriculum Grades K to 6 corresponds with ages:
language.howToChooseYourGradeContent:
It’s very important children start at the right level, have fun in learning and work at their own pace. Please help the children selecting the level that is not too easy, but also not too difficult for them. There are two ways to do this.

  • You can either check the learning goals yourself to determine the correct level for your child(ren).
  • Or you can let the child take several lessons to determine his or her level. For example, if your child has the age of 6, please let him or her take one lesson in grade K, one lesson in grade 1, and one lesson in grade 2 to determine at which level he or she is.

dialog.text: Hello, I am Tim.
Hello! My name is Martin Olsen and I’m visiting my grandparents. They own a fishing shop right near the Arctic Ocean in Iceland.
The shop uses a lot of electricity. Look at the lights on the ceiling. They use electricity to work. The lights are controlled by the light switch on the wall.
My grandpa, Harry, knows everything about electricity. He’s going to explain how the switches control the lights. Would you like to come along? Great, let’s go!
Many things rely on electricity to run. Help Martin learn how electrical currents flow through different objects in the store and on the boat.

It’s the same for all things that use electricity. Lights shine brighter with more power and the toaster toasts bread faster.

You'll need to be careful when dealing with electricity. Some materials conduct electricity, like copper wire. These materials are called conductors.
Other materials block electricity, like plastic or rubber. These materials are called insulators.
The difference is that conductors allow electrical current to flow easily, for example wires and metal.
Electrical insulators oppose the flow of electricity, for example, rubber, glass, and paper.
Will you help me determine which of the items I show you, are electrical conductors or electrical insulators?
